newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak ZSNP sees minor impact in energy price rise.
newsitem.headline: Slovak ZSNP sees minor impact in energy price rise.

text.p: Slovak aluminium maker ZSNP a.s. said on Wednesday it saw little impact from a recent hike in energy prices, as it had a special delivery contract with the country's electricity monopoly.

"We have a 10-year contract with Slovenske Elektrarne, signed in 1994, according to which we receive power at the constant price of three cents per kilowatt," ZSNP economic director Tibor Brasen told Reuters.

He added that the special contract includes only the most heavily energy-consuming electrolysis units in ZSNP's main subsidiary, Slovalco a.s., while other parts of the holding would be affected by the new electricity price.
"However, the increase in our costs (of the entire holding) should not exceed five million crowns annually," Brasen said.
Earlier this summer, the finance ministry approved a proposal by Slovenske Elektrarne a.s. to raise electricity prices by 10 percent for corporate customers from August 1.
But Brasen said ZSNP would not be able to raise prices and would have to seek other solutions.
"We can't move the aluminium price, as it is generated by the world market," he said, adding the company was seeking measures to increase productivity and cut expenditure.

In 1993, ZSNP restructured itself into a holding company, setting up the Slovalco smelter with equity participation from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Hydro Aluminium, a subsidiary of Norsk Hydro of Norway.
Norsk Hydro and the EBRD each have a 10 percent stake in Slovalco, while ZSNP holds the remaining 80 percent.

ZSNP, state-controlled through a 74-percent stake held by the state privatisation agency, was placed on the list of Slovak strategic companies in which the state would retain a "golden share" with veto power.
Economics ministry officials say the impact of the energy price hike on the entire industrial sector remains unclear.
"There are no overall estimates, as we don't have the appropriate information from every company," Jozef Sucha, spokesman of the Economics Ministry, told Reuters.
Last month, Economics Minister Karol Cesnek said the price hike was expected to boost producer prices by an average "two to three percentage points".
